title: What an antibody recognizes
objective: Define an epitope and explain what determines antibody specificity.

steps.title: Antibodies see shapes, not names
steps.body: An **[[antibody]]** binds one small patch on its target — an **[[epitope]]**, a specific 3D shape of a few amino acids. It doesn't know the protein's name; it only recognizes that shape. Change the shape (denaturation, fixation, a point mutation) and binding can fail.

steps.prompt: What does an antibody actually bind?
options: An epitope — a small, specific region on the target
A whole protein, recognized somehow by its function
The gene sequence that encodes the target protein
Any protein that happens to be roughly the right size
steps.explanation: Antibodies bind epitopes — small shaped regions. That's why one protein can have several antibodies against different epitopes.

variants.setup: Two antibodies are raised against the same protein but different regions.
variants.prompt: Can they give different staining patterns?
options: Yes, if the two epitopes differ in accessibility
No, the same protein always stains identically
Only if one of the two antibodies is polyclonal
variants.reveal: Different epitopes can be differently accessible after fixation, so the same protein can stain differently with two antibodies.

steps.setup: An antibody works well on fresh-frozen sections. You use it on heavily cross-linked, PFA-fixed tissue.
options: Stronger binding than on fresh tissue
Binding may fail because the epitope is masked or altered
Same binding, since fixation just locks the target in place
steps.reveal: Fixation can distort or bury the epitope. This is exactly why antigen retrieval and the right fixation (C6) matter.

variants.prompt: Heavy fixation can make an antibody fail because it…
options: Alters or buries the epitope's shape
Washes the target protein out of the tissue
Breaks the target into small fragments
variants.explanation: Cross-linking can distort the epitope the antibody needs.

steps.title: Monoclonal vs polyclonal
steps.body: A **monoclonal** antibody recognizes one epitope (consistent, specific, but fragile if that epitope is hidden). A **polyclonal** is a mix recognizing several epitopes on the target (robust signal, but more batch-to-batch variation and off-target risk).

reviewNotes: Epitope concept; sets up IF mechanics and validation.
